1.title: Know the parts of a computer and a network
1.intro: IT support starts with knowing what is inside a computer and how devices join a network.
pts: Name the main parts: processor, memory, storage, screen, battery and ports.
Explain what the operating system does and how it differs from an app.
Explain what a router, Wi-Fi and an internet provider each do.
Name common devices: laptop, phone, printer and tablet.
Say the difference between hardware, software and settings.
1.ex: A user says 'the internet is down'. You ask: is it one device or all? If only one device fails, the problem is likely in that device, not the router.
1.act: Draw a home network with five devices and label each part's job.
1.std: Task: draw and label a network. Condition: one real or practice network. Standard: every device and link is named and its job is stated in one sentence.

2.title: Listen, ask and write the problem down
2.intro: Most fixes start with a clear description. Good support asks short questions and writes the answers.
pts: Ask: what did you try to do, what happened, what did you expect, when did it start?
Ask if anything changed recently, such as an update or a new device.
Write a ticket with date, user, device, problem and steps tried.
Use plain words and avoid blaming the user.
Tell the user what you will do next and how long it may take.
2.ex: Ticket: 'Printer not printing. Started this morning after an update. Other computers print fine. Tried restarting the printer.' The note already points to a computer setting.
2.act: Role-play three support calls and write a ticket for each.
2.std: Task: write three tickets. Condition: practice calls with a partner. Standard: each ticket has the five facts, plain words and a next step.

3.title: Fix common problems step by step
3.intro: Use a fixed order: check the simple things, change one thing at a time, and test.
pts: Check power, cables, Wi-Fi and storage space before deeper steps.
Restart the device and the app; many faults clear.
Change one thing at a time and write it down.
Check for pending updates and free disk space.
Know when to stop and escalate to a person with more skill.
3.ex: A laptop is slow. Disk is 98% full. You clear downloads with the user's consent and remove unused programs. Speed returns, and you note the cause.
3.act: Fix five practice faults on a spare device and record each step.
3.std: Task: fix five faults. Condition: a spare or practice device. Standard: each fix has the steps, the test that proves it and the cause.

4.title: Keep data and accounts safe
4.intro: Support staff see private data. Keep accounts safe and handle data with care.
pts: Explain strong passwords, a password manager and two-step sign-in.
Spot a phishing message: odd sender, urgent tone, strange link, request for a password.
Never ask users to tell you their password; reset it with them instead.
Explain Canada's privacy rules: federal and provincial laws apply to personal information; Quebec has its own law.
Report a suspected data leak to the responsible person quickly; check the current rule on breach reporting with the privacy regulator.
4.ex: A user gets an email saying 'your account will close in one hour'. You check the link without opening it and see the address is not the real one. You advise deleting it and reporting it.
4.act: Make a one-page safe-use guide for non-experts and a five-line phishing checklist.
4.std: Task: write a safety guide. Condition: plain words, one page. Standard: covers passwords, two-step sign-in, phishing and who to tell when something goes wrong.

5.title: Back up, update and set up devices
5.intro: Setup and care prevent most problems. Teach users the habits too.
pts: Set up a backup that runs on a schedule, and test a restore at least once.
Turn on automatic updates where safe and plan restarts at quiet times.
Set up a new user: account, access level, email, printer and Wi-Fi.
Remove access when a person leaves.
Keep a list of devices, who uses them and when they were bought.
5.ex: A small office has no backup. You set a nightly backup to external storage and a copy to a second place. You then restore one file to prove it works.
5.act: Set up a backup and restore one file on a practice device.
5.std: Task: back up and restore. Condition: a practice device. Standard: the backup runs on schedule, one restore works and a written note says where copies are.

6.title: Price support and write simple terms
6.intro: A support business sells time and trust. Price covers your time, travel and tools.
pts: Choose a price model: per hour, per visit or a monthly plan.
Count unpaid time: travel, tickets, learning and admin.
Write terms: what is covered, response time, payment date and what is out of scope.
Ask a licensed adviser about insurance and sales tax.
Offer a plan for a small group with a fixed monthly fee.
6.ex: A monthly plan for a five-person office is 250 CAD. You expect 3 hours a month at 40 CAD cost per hour = 120. Margin 130 CAD, about 52%, before overhead.
6.act: Build a price sheet and a one-page terms document.
6.std: Task: price and write terms. Condition: a spreadsheet. Standard: formulas show cost and margin and the terms list scope, response time and exclusions.

7.title: Work with small businesses and community
7.intro: Many clients are households, seniors and small shops. Help them stay safe and keep things simple.
pts: Explain things in short steps and let users try it themselves.
Write a one-page how-to with screenshots for common jobs.
Respect accessibility needs such as larger text or a screen reader.
Offer help in English, French or another language you can use well.
Keep a log of all visits for later review.
7.ex: A senior wants video calls. You set up one icon on the screen, write a three-step card and practise twice with her until she can start the call alone.
7.act: Create a one-page how-to for a common task and test it with a real user.
7.std: Task: write a how-to. Condition: one real user. Standard: the user completes the task alone using only the page.

8.title: Run an IT support service for real
8.intro: Now run it: track tickets, measure quality and improve.
pts: Track tickets: opened, closed, time to first reply and time to fix.
Spot repeat problems and fix the cause once.
Keep a runbook for the three most likely faults.
Set a review each month with the client.
Write a 12-month plan with milestones and a budget.
8.ex: Over 30 days a service closes 40 tickets. Eleven are 'password reset'. A short self-help page cuts these to four the next month.
8.act: Run a 60-day pilot with real or practice clients and write the review.
8.std: Task: run a support pilot. Condition: 60 days. Standard: tickets are logged, repeat causes are found and the review gives decisions with evidence.

quiz: What are the five facts for a good ticket?
Date, user, device, problem and steps tried.
Why change only one thing at a time?
So you know which change fixed or broke it.
Why test a restore?
A backup you have never restored may not work when needed.
Name two signs of a phishing message.
An odd sender and an urgent request, a strange link or a request for a password.
Should you ask users to tell you their password?
No; reset it with them instead.
What does the operating system do?
It runs the device and lets apps use its parts.
What first checks come before deeper fixes?
Power, cables, Wi-Fi and storage space.
What should happen when a person leaves a business?
Their access is removed.
When should you escalate a problem?
When it is beyond your skill or risk is high.
What do you do if you are unsure of a privacy rule?
Check the current rule with the privacy regulator or a licensed adviser.
